1H (Number Theory)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 140
1H OurBigBook.com
Let p1​,…,pa​ be the first a primes, and let ϕ(x,a) count positive integers at most x not divisible by any of them. The inclusion-exclusion principle gives
ϕ(x,a)=∑S⊆{1,…,a}​(−1)∣S∣⌊∏j∈S​pj​x​⌋.
(1)
For a=π(x​), every composite at most x is removed, so the survivors are one and the primes larger than x​. Thus the Legendre prime-counting formula is π(x)=ϕ(x,π(x​))+π(x​)−1​. This is the prime-counting formula, distinct from the factorial-valuation formula of the same name.
Fix y≥2 and put a=π(y). Every prime exceeding y is among the unsieved integers. Replacing each floor in the finite sum by its argument makes an error bounded by 2a, giving
π(x)≤a+ϕ(x,a)≤a+x∏p≤y​(1−1/p)+2a.
(2)
Take x→∞ with y fixed. The supplied product estimate gives 0≤limsupπ(x)/x≤1/logy. Since y can be arbitrarily large, x→∞lim​π(x)/x=0​. The order of these limits avoids treating the growing inclusion-exclusion error as negligible.

For each node define its Lagrange interpolation cardinal polynomial ℓi​(t)=∏j=i​(t−xj​)/(xi​−xj​). Its square has degree 2n−2<2n and nodal values ℓi​(xj​)2=δij​. Exactness therefore gives ai​=∫−11​ℓi​(t)2dt. The polynomial is nonzero, so continuity makes this integral strictly positive. Thus ai​>0​ for every node.

iii

Words: 80 Articles: 1
2F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 80
iii OurBigBook.com
Put P(t)=∏i​(t−xi​). For every polynomial q of degree at most n−1, Pq has degree at most 2n−1 and vanishes at all nodes; thus ∫−11​Pq=0. The monic degree-n orthogonal polynomial for this integral is unique: the difference of two such monic polynomials has degree below n and is orthogonal to itself, hence is zero. Consequently P is the monic normalization of the degree-n Legendre polynomial, proving the given nodes are exactly its roots. Together the three results characterize this Gaussian quadrature rule.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 247 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 247
3G OurBigBook.com
A nonidentity Möbius transformation has either two distinct fixed points on the Riemann sphere or one double fixed point. With two fixed points, conjugate them to zero and infinity. A Möbius map fixing both is z↦kz with k=0. With one fixed point, conjugate it to infinity; the resulting map is affine, z↦az+b. If a=1 it would have another fixed point, so a=1 and b=0. Scaling the coordinate makes it z↦z+1. The identity is already the case k=1.
Define tr2(g) using a determinant-one representing matrix; the two possible lifts differ by sign, so its square is well defined and invariant under conjugation. For z↦kz it is k+2+k−1, while for a nontrivial translation it is four. If two nonidentity dilations have equal trace-square, their multipliers satisfy the same quadratic and are either equal or reciprocal. Inversion z↦1/z conjugates one reciprocal multiplier to the other. Trace-square four forces the dilation multiplier to be one, which is the excluded identity; thus every nonidentity map with that invariant is in the translation class. This proves g∼h⟺tr2(g)=tr2(h)​ for the stated nonidentity maps.
Not every such map fixes an interior point of hyperbolic three-space. In its upper-half-space extension, z↦z+1 translates the horizontal coordinate and has no fixed point at positive height. A dilation extends as (z,t)↦(kz,∣k∣t), so it fixes the vertical axis only when ∣k∣=1; if ∣k∣=1, the height changes. Boundary fixed points therefore do not imply an interior fixed point.

4J (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 172 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 172
4J OurBigBook.com
A digital signature lets a holder of a private key authenticate a message while anyone with the public key verifies it. Signing a message digest ties the signature to the message and detects alterations; it does not conceal the message. Authentication also requires a trustworthy association of the public key with its owner.
For the ElGamal signature scheme, choose a large prime p and a generator g of Fp×​. The secret is x, and the public key is (p,g,y) with y=gxmodp. To sign a message whose hash is represented by mmod(p−1), choose a fresh secret nonce k coprime to p−1 and set
r=gkmodp,s=k−1(m−xr)mod(p−1).​
(3)
Transmit (r,s) with the message. Verification checks the permitted ranges and gm≡yrrs(modp)​. Correctness follows from xr+ks≡m(modp−1). The secret exponent prevents an outsider from directly constructing this relation for an arbitrary hashed message; nonce reuse can expose the exponent through the repeated linear congruences. Hashing is part of the signature scheme, rather than signing arbitrary raw exponents with no message encoding.

β​=(XTX)−1XTY=β+(XTX)−1XTϵ.

The probability of an exact copy is Q=qL. Incorrect copies contribute mutants at rate a(1−Q)x, giving y˙​=by+a(1−Q)x​. For y>0, differentiating the ratio gives
z˙=(aQ−b)z−a(1−Q)z2.​
(6)

b OurBigBook.com
For 0<q<1, a finite positive equilibrium exists exactly when aqL>b, and then
z∗​=(aqL−b)/[a(1−qL)].​
(7)
The derivative of the ratio's vector field at z∗​ is −(aqL−b)<0, so this equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable; every positive initial ratio tends to it. The critical real length is Lc​=log(b/a)/logq, and the admissible integer lengths satisfy L<Lc​. Thus the largest positive integer length, if one exists, is Lmax​=⌈Lc​⌉−1​. At equality the equilibrium is zero, so rounding down without accounting for the strict inequality can be wrong. If q=1, mutants are never produced from masters and the ratio grows without a finite positive equilibrium; the finite threshold formula concerns imperfect copying.

Lc​≃1−qs​.​
(8)
The largest permitted integer is still selected by the strict inequality from part (b). This says that longer master sequences need a proportionately larger selective advantage or smaller per-digit copying error.

7B (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 135
7B OurBigBook.com
At a hyperbolic saddle, the stable invariant subspace of Df(0) is the sum of its generalized eigenspaces with negative real parts; the unstable subspace uses positive real parts. The stable manifold theorem gives invariant local manifolds tangent to these subspaces at the equilibrium, with the corresponding dimensions and the appropriate forward or backward convergence to the equilibrium.
Here the Jacobian is diag(1,−1), so the unstable tangent is the x axis and the stable tangent the y axis. For the stable graph write x=h(y)=Ay2+By3+O(y4). Invariance requires h′(y)(−y+3h(y)2)=h+h2+2hy+3y2. Comparing quadratic and cubic terms gives −2A=A+3 and −3B=B+2A, so A=−1,B=1/2.
For the unstable graph y=g(x)=Cx2+Dx3+O(x4), invariance is g′(x)(x+x2+2xg+3g2)=−g+3x2. Coefficients give 2C=3−C and 2C+3D=−D, so C=1,D=−1/2. Thus the cubic graph expansion of a saddle invariant manifold is
Ws: x=−y2+y3/2+O(y4),Wu: y=x2−x3/2+O(x4).​
(9)
These describe the local manifolds to cubic order, not exact global polynomial curves.

h(p)​=∫0∞​∫0u​e−puf(u−v)g(v)dvdu=∫0∞​∫0∞​e−p(t+v)f(t)g(v)dtdv=f​(p)g​(p)​.​

For the specified inverse-square-root function, the supplied identity says f∗f=π on t>0. Consequently f​(p)2=π/p. For real p>0 the defining integral is positive, fixing the positive square root; analytic continuation into Rep>0 gives
f​(p)=π​p−1/2,​

with the branch positive on the positive real axis. The square identity alone would not select the sign.

a

Words: 118 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 118
a OurBigBook.com
For a homogeneous isotropic metric, radial light propagation covers comoving distance ∫cdt/a(t). The physical particle horizon is dp​(t)=a(t)∫ti​t​cdt′/a(t′), when this is finite. A future event horizon exists when de​(t)=a(t)∫ttf​​cdt′/a(t′) is finite. The Hubble radius is the instantaneous scale c/H, with H=a˙/a; it is not generally the same as either causal horizon.
For an Einstein-de Sitter universe, H=2/(3t), so c/H=3ct/2, while dp​=3ct from a beginning at zero. The future integral diverges, so there is no event horizon. For an eternal-past de Sitter spacetime, H is constant and the particle-horizon integral from −∞ diverges. Its event horizon and Hubble radius both equal c/H. Thus a Hubble radius is not automatically a particle horizon, even in these simple isotropic models.

b

Words: 127 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 127
b OurBigBook.com
For an expanding decelerating power law a∝tα with 0<α<1, the particle horizon is ct/(1−α), and the comoving Hubble radius is c/(aH)∝t1−α. It increases with time, so regions that are mutually visible today can have been out of causal contact at early times. The nearly uniform early thermal conditions inferred across such regions give the horizon problem.
During cosmic inflation, accelerated expansion makes the comoving Hubble radius decrease. A patch initially within one causal communication scale can expand into the region now observed, after which its separated parts are temporarily outside the Hubble radius and later re-enter during deceleration. Sufficient duration before the hot radiation era permits a common causal origin; accelerated expansion is not itself a claim that signals propagate faster than light locally.

For the radiation-era law beginning at tr​, the present particle-horizon estimate is
dH​(t0​)=2ct0​(1−tr​/t0​​)≃2ct0​≃6×1025 m.
(14)
Rescale this present physical distance back to tr​ using a(tr​)/a(t0​)=tr​/t0​​. Its physical size was 2ctr​t0​​≃0.6 m, of order one metre as required. The matched inflationary Hubble rate is H=1/(2tr​)≃5×1034 s−1, with Hubble radius c/H≃6×10−27 m.
If inflation produces N e-folds before tr​, this patch began with size 0.6e−N metres. It fits within one Hubble radius if
eN≳1026,N≳26log10≃60.​
(15)
This estimate uses the idealized radiation-only history stated in the question; substituting the actual matter-dominated history would change the numerical estimate.

11H (Number Theory)

Words: 243 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 243
11H OurBigBook.com
Write a reduced positive definite binary quadratic form as [a,b,c]=ax2+bxy+cy2, with ∣b∣≤a≤c and b≥0 on the reduction boundaries. Since 4ac−b2=20, reduction gives 3a2≤20, so a=1 or two. The middle coefficient is even. For a=1, only b=0 is possible, yielding c=5. For a=2, b=0 would give a noninteger c, while b=±2 gives c=3; the boundary convention selects b=2. Thus the two reduced forms are
x2+5y2,2x2+2xy+3y2.​
(16)
A positive odd integer n is properly represented by some integer form of discriminant d exactly when b2≡d(mod4n) has a solution. For a specified proper equivalence class, the more precise criterion is that [n,b,(b2−d)/(4n)] belong to that class for some such b. Indeed, a primitive representing vector extends to an SL2​(Z) basis change, making the leading coefficient n; conversely that form represents n at the primitive vector (1,0).
For primes p∤10, the existence criterion is (−20/p)=1, because the congruence modulo four is compatible with an even middle coefficient. Quadratic reciprocity gives (−20/p)=(−1/p)(p/5), so the split possibilities are p≡1,3,7,9(mod20). Any proper representing form reduces to one of the two listed forms. Odd values of x2+5y2 are one modulo four; odd values of 2x2+2xy+3y2 require odd y and are three modulo four. These distinguish the two classes. Consequently
p=x2+5y2 for a prime p=2,5⟺p≡1 or 9(mod20).​
(17)
A representation of a prime is automatically proper: a common divisor of x,y would have its square divide p.

12J (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 266 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 266
12J OurBigBook.com
A linear length-n cyclic code is a subspace closed under cyclic coordinate shifts. Identify a word with its polynomial modulo Xn−1; multiplying by X performs the shift. Thus a cyclic code is an ideal of Fq​[X]/(Xn−1). Its preimage in the polynomial ring is an ideal containing Xn−1, so the Euclidean algorithm gives a unique monic generator g dividing Xn−1. The generator polynomial of a cyclic code is g and the check polynomial of a cyclic code is h=(Xn−1)/g; a word lies in the code exactly when hc≡0(modXn−1).
For the binary length-seven code, the given h factors with
g(X)=X3+X+1,(X3+X+1)(X4+X2+X+1)=X7+1.​
(18)
This cubic has no binary root and is irreducible. Let α be its root in F8​. Since the nonzero multiplicative group has prime order seven and α=1, its seven powers enumerate all nonzero elements. The condition c(α)=0 gives a three-row binary parity-check matrix whose columns are precisely the seven nonzero vectors of F23​. This is Hamming's code in a cyclic coordinate order. It has dimension four, and minimum distance three: no one or two distinct nonzero columns sum to zero, while g itself has weight three. Its sixteen radius-one balls have total size 16(1+7)=128, confirming the original perfect Hamming code.
It actually contains its dual code in this coordinate order. Each parity-check row has four ones, and any two distinct rows have two simultaneous ones, so HHT=0 over F2​. The row space C⊥ therefore lies in kerH=C. Equivalently the dual generator is the reciprocal check polynomial
h∗(X)=X4+X3+X2+1=(X+1)g(X),
(19)
which is divisible by g. Hence there is a three-dimensional subcode equal to the dual, and in any other coordinate order it is equivalent to that dual.

η22ext​=β1​+β2​β2​​η11​.​

Writing τi​=1/βi​, its factor is τ1​/(τ1​+τ2​). Slow environmental changes are followed almost fully; rapid environmental fluctuations are averaged over the longer protein response time. Thus extrinsic noise is the magnitude of relative RNA fluctuations multiplied by a dynamical averaging factor.

Factor the extrinsic term as
η22ext​≃η11​H21​β1​+β2​Hβ2​H​.​
(26)
The first factor is environmental relative variance. The second is static susceptibility squared: differentiating the equilibrium relation gives δlogm2​=H−1δlogm1​. The last is the time-averaging factor with effective protein response time 1/(β2​H). Feedback makes response faster, which by itself weakens averaging, but simultaneously reduces the static gain. These are distinct effects and both must be retained.

e

Words: 120 Articles: 1
13E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
e OurBigBook.com
For the constitutive system, every propensity is affine in the copy numbers. The exact first- and second-moment equations therefore close: expectations of drift are determined by the means, and covariance drift by the covariance. The stationary fluctuation-dissipation calculation is consequently exact, even though the full joint stationary distribution need not be Gaussian.
For feedback, expectations such as E[x1​f(x2​)] involve nonlinear moments and correlations. Replacing them by a linear expansion about the mean is a linear noise approximation, so the covariance formula is approximate. It works well around a stable single equilibrium when relative fluctuations are small and the rates vary smoothly over their typical range, generally at sufficiently large molecule numbers. Low counts, strong nonlinearities, multiple attractors and proximity to instability can invalidate it.

f

Words: 134 Articles: 1
13E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 134
f OurBigBook.com
With response rates and elasticity effectively fixed, changing λ2​ changes m2​ and hence intrinsic noise but not the environmental term. Observation (i) therefore indicates extrinsic noise dominates, making the mean-dependent intrinsic contribution negligible. For a general feedback law whose elasticity changes substantially with the mean, compensation between terms is another possibility; independence from λ2​ alone would then not logically identify the dominant term.
Observation (ii) measures the local relaxation rate β2​H, which is larger under negative feedback. Observation (iii) is not explained by faster adjustment alone. At fixed susceptibility, increasing the response rate increases β2​H/(β1​+β2​H), reducing time averaging and increasing transmitted environmental noise. Feedback lowers variance primarily by reducing susceptibility and the intrinsic term. Thus rapid adjustment and low noise share a feedback mechanism but are not a direct causal equivalence.

The Axiom of foundation states that every nonempty set A has a member a disjoint from A. The principle of membership induction states that a property P satisfying ∀x[(∀y∈x P(y))⇒P(x)] holds for every set.
Assume Foundation and suppose a progressive property fails at a set x. In the transitive closure of {x}, form the nonempty set of counterexamples by Separation. Foundation selects a counterexample a with no counterexample among its members. Transitivity makes those members belong to the closure, so each satisfies P, and progressiveness gives P(a), a contradiction. Conversely, if a nonempty A had no member disjoint from it, the property P(x):x∈/A would be progressive: a member of A necessarily has a member in A. Membership induction would then say no set belongs to A, a contradiction. Thus Foundation and membership induction are equivalent.
Apply induction to the property that a set belongs to some stage of the cumulative hierarchy. For each member y of x, choose its least stage ordinal. Replacement collects these ordinals into a set; take an ordinal γ large enough that all members lie in Vγ​. Then x⊆Vγ​ and x∈Vγ+1​. This proves every set appears in the hierarchy.
For finite stages let an​=∣Vn​∣. Then a0​=0,an+1​=2an​​, giving 0,1,2,4,16,65536,…. The stage Vω​ is countably infinite, as the union of the finite stages. Thus ∣Vω+1​∣=2ℵ0​=∣R∣. Cantor's theorem makes ∣Vω+2​∣ strictly larger, and every later stage contains it. Earlier stages have at most countable size. Therefore ∣Vα​∣=∣R∣⟺α=ω+1​.

Irreducibility modulo two makes the rational quartic irreducible, and its rational Galois group is transitive on four roots. The unramified factorization theorem supplies a four-cycle from the modulo-two reduction and a three-cycle from the modulo-three reduction. Its order is divisible by twelve and divides twenty-four. A Bayes estimator minimizes the prior-averaged risk, or equivalently minimizes posterior expected loss at almost every observation. An admissible rule has no competing rule of no greater risk everywhere and strictly smaller risk somewhere. To construct a Bayes rule, form the posterior and minimize its expected loss over the allowed actions. Under squared error and finite posterior second moments the unique action is the posterior mean.
Put S=∣X∣2. The given fourth moment and independence give Ev​S=nv, Ev​S2=n(n+2)v2. Thus
R(v,αS)=v2[n(n+2)α2−2nα+1]=v2[n(n+2)(α−n+21​)2+n+22​].

Every α=1/(n+2) is strictly dominated at every v>0 by that coefficient. Hence it cannot be a finite-risk Bayes rule for any proper prior.
To make the second requested comparison, let mj​=Eπ​vj and assume finite quadratic Bayes risk. For the affine rules the integrated risk is
r(α,β)=[n(n+2)α2−2nα+1]m2​+2β(nα−1)m1​+β2.

But the marginal density of S would then be a constant times sn/2−2−1/(2α), a pure power not integrable at both zero and infinity. This contradicts a proper prior's normalized predictive distribution. This is the proper-prior obstruction to homogeneous variance Bayes rules.
The finite-loss qualification matters: allowing all posterior losses to equal infinity makes every action a vacuous minimizer. A different constant noise intensity multiplies C but leaves the control unchanged, as in the terminal-position reduction of double-integrator control.

Watson lemma expands a Laplace integral by integrating the small-t expansion term by term. More precisely, if f(t)∼∑j≥0​aj​tλ+j−1 with Reλ>0, and the tail satisfies bounds permitting this localization, then
∫0∞​e−xtf(t)dt∼∑j≥0​aj​Γ(λ+j)x−λ−j.
(52)
For ordinary powers f(t)∼∑cj​tj, the coefficients are cj​j!. For the Gaussian weight, put s=t2 separately on the positive and negative half-lines. The integral becomes a Laplace integral with amplitude [f(s​)+f(−s​)]/(2s​). Odd terms cancel and Watson lemma gives
∫−∞∞​e−xt2f(t)dt∼∑j≥0​c2j​Γ(j+21​)x−j−1/2.
(53)
These assertions concern asymptotic expansions, not necessarily convergent series.
For the complex integral in the lower half-plane, the identity (z−t)−1=i∫0∞​e−i(z−t)sds and the Gaussian Fourier transform give
I(z)=iπ​∫0∞​e−s2/4−izsds=iπe−z2erfc(iz)​.
(54)
The last expression, initially obtained by completing the square, is entire and therefore gives the requested analytic continuation. Expanding the denominator formally, with odd Gaussian moments zero, gives the algebraic expansion
A(z)=zπ​​∑j≥0​(2z2)j(2j−1)!!​=zπ​​(1+2z21​+4z43​+⋯).
(55)
Here (−1)!!=1. The complementary error function expansion shows I(z)∼A(z) on closed subsectors of −5π/4<argz<π/4, using an unwrapped argument centered on the lower half-plane.
In the upper half-plane, the directly evaluated real-contour integral is J(z)=−iπe−z2erfc(−iz). Since erfc(w)+erfc(−w)=2, continuation from below gives
I(z)=J(z)+2πie−z2,I(z)∼A(z)+2πie−z2.​
(56)
The upper expansion for J holds on closed subsectors of −π/4<argz<5π/4. The added term is the residue acquired by the continued contour passing the pole; it is exponentially dominant in the upper sector π/4<argz<3π/4 and exponentially small near either real ray. On the real axis the continued value is the principal-value integral plus iπe−x2.
To make the Stokes phenomenon convention explicit, the exponential switches its asymptotic multiplier across the real rays argz=0,π; these are the Stokes switching lines. The diagonal rays argz=π/4+jπ/2 separate exponential growth from decay and are often called anti-Stokes lines, or critical boundaries when regions are classified by dominance. Thus both sets of critical directions and the exact jump are specified, independently of which terminology is used. This is the Gaussian Cauchy transform and its Stokes jump.

There is a literal inconsistency in the stated Riemann-Hilbert problem: a jump matrix S(k) tending to zero is incompatible with μ±​→I. Along the real axis the conjugating exponentials are unitary, so the right side of the jump tends to zero while the left side tends to I. No normalized solution satisfies the printed decay condition. The intended condition is S(k)→I, or replacement of S in the jump by I+S when S denotes its decaying part.
For this corrected problem assume a regular, invertible, pole-free solution, differentiable in x,t, with the required expansion uniformly at infinity. These conditions matter: arbitrary jump data need not be solvable, and poles would contribute extra terms. Write σ=σ3​ and μ=I+μ1​/k+μ2​/k2+⋯. Matching the nondecaying coefficients in the two differential expressions yields
Q=i[σ,μ1​],A=2i[σ,μ1​]=2Q,B=2i[σ,μ2​]−Aμ1​.​
(57)
The first expression makes Q off-diagonal.
These matches really establish the differential equations, rather than just formal identities. Let G=e−i(kx+2k2t)σS(k)ei(kx+2k2t)σ. It satisfies Gx​=−ik[σ,G] and Gt​=−2ik2[σ,G]. Differentiating μ+​=μ−​G consequently shows that
Rx​=(μx​+ik[σ,μ]−Qμ)μ−1,Rt​=(μt​+2ik2[σ,μ]−(kA+B)μ)μ−1
(58)
have matching boundary values. They therefore extend holomorphically across the contour. The chosen coefficients make both residuals O(k−1) at infinity. Their absence of poles and Liouville theorem imply Rx​=Rt​=0, proving the required Lax pair under the corrected hypotheses. This is matrix NLS reconstruction from a normalized Riemann-Hilbert problem.

Addition of two spin-one angular momenta gives J=0,1,2, with M=−J,−J+1,…,J. To obtain the J=1 multiplet, its highest-weight state must have M=1 and be killed by J+​=J+(1)​+J+(2)​. On the two possible product states, the raising operator gives the same multiple of ∣1;1⟩, so their difference is required. Normalization and successive lowering give
∣1,1⟩∣1,0⟩∣1,−1⟩​=2​∣1;0⟩−∣0;1⟩​,=2​∣1;−1⟩−∣−1;1⟩​,=2​∣0;−1⟩−∣−1;0⟩​.​​
(64)
For example J−​∣1,1⟩=∣1;−1⟩−∣−1;1⟩=2​∣1,0⟩, and lowering once more gives the last expression. These states are all antisymmetric under interchanging the two constituents.
Identical spin-one particles are bosons, so the total state must be symmetric. Its J=1 spin factor is antisymmetric and must therefore multiply an antisymmetric spatial factor. Two particles in the same one-particle orbital have zero antisymmetric spatial state. The lowest allowed choice is
2​ψ1​(rA​)ψ2​(rB​)−ψ2​(rA​)ψ1​(rB​)​∣1,M⟩,E=E1​+E2​​,M=−1,0,1.
(65)
For distinguishable particles there is no exchange-symmetry constraint. Both can occupy the ground orbital, giving ψ1​(rA​)ψ1​(rB​)∣1,M⟩ and lowest energy 2E1​​, again with three spin states.

A Bravais lattice is the set of all integer combinations of linearly independent primitive translation vectors. Its reciprocal lattice consists of g satisfying g⋅l∈2πZ for every translation l; equivalently eig⋅l=1.
The original PDF's third family has a bare j, not n2​j. Taken literally, the listed set is not the claimed Bravais lattice: the claimed primitive vector a(i+k)/2 does not occur. Its half-integer first and third coordinates force it into that third family, whose second coordinate is always a, not zero. The intended repair is j↦n2​j in the third family. The following conclusions apply to that corrected set.
The four corrected families are exactly
L=2a​{(h,k,l)∈Z3:h+k+l is even}.
(66)
The allowed parity patterns are all even, or exactly two odd coordinates. An integer combination of the proposed primitive vectors has coordinates (a/2)(m2​+m3​,m1​+m3​,m1​+m2​), so lies in this set. Conversely, solve
m1​=21​(k+l−h),m2​=21​(h+l−k),m3​=21​(h+k−l).
(67)
All three are integers precisely when h+k+l is even. This proves that the corrected set is the face-centered cubic lattice with the proposed primitive basis.
Direct dot products give ai​⋅bj​=2πδij​ for
b1​=a2π​(−1,1,1),b2​=a2π​(1,−1,1),b3​=a2π​(1,1,−1).​
(68)
These vectors generate the entire reciprocal lattice, since the coefficients of an arbitrary reciprocal vector in this basis are its integer pairings with the ai​. Its vectors are (2π/a)(h,k,l) with all three coordinates of the same parity, the body-centered cubic lattice.
In Bragg scattering, translating a scattering atom by l changes the amplitude by ei(k−k′)⋅l. Constructive interference from every lattice translate requires this factor to be one, so k′−k=g is a reciprocal lattice vector. For elastic scattering, ∣k′∣=∣k∣; the chord between these two vectors has length 2∣k∣sin(θ/2). Therefore
sin(θ/2)=2∣k∣∣g∣​.​
(69)
The shortest nonzero reciprocal vectors are the (111) family of length (2π/a)3​, followed by the (200) family of length (2π/a)2. Identical atoms on this Bravais lattice introduce no additional basis extinction. If both families are accessible at the incident wavelength, their scattering angles obey sin(θ1​/2)/sin(θ2​/2)=3​/2​.

The incompressible Navier-Stokes equations are ut​+(u⋅∇)u=−∇p/ρ+νΔu and ∇⋅u=0, with no penetration and no slip at a stationary rigid wall. The Euler limit takes ν→0 at fixed distance from the wall, leaving the inviscid Euler equations and a no-penetration condition; imposing tangential no slip on that outer problem generally overdetermines it. The Prandtl limit resolves a shrinking wall layer in which transverse viscous diffusion remains comparable to convection and restores no slip.
For the steady flat-plate boundary layer, δ/x≪1, continuity makes v/U=O(δ/x), and uxx​ is small compared with uyy​. Normal momentum makes pressure independent of y to leading order. The constant outer speed makes the outer pressure gradient, and hence px​ throughout the layer, zero. The leading equations are uux​+vuy​=νuyy​ and ux​+vy​=0. With the stream function convention u=ψy​, v=−ψx​, these give
ψy​ψxy​−ψx​ψyy​=νψyyy​.
(77)
Balancing U2/x against νU/δ2 gives δ=νx/U​. There is no independent streamwise scale for the semi-infinite plate, motivating the similarity solution
η=yνxU​​,ψ=νUx​f(η).​
(78)
It gives u=Uf′ and v=21​νU/x​(ηf′−f). Substitution yields uux​+vuy​=−U2ff′′/(2x) and νuyy​=U2f′′′/x, so the Blasius equation and conditions are
f′′′+21​ff′′=0,f(0)=f′(0)=0,f′(∞)=1.​
(79)
The first two conditions impose no penetration and no slip; the last matches the outer stream.
The wall shear on one face is τ(x)=ρνuy​(x,0)=ρUνU/x​f′′(0). Integration from zero to L gives 2ρU2Lf′′(0)/UL/ν​ on one face. With the same flow on both faces, the total drag force per unit width is
F=UL/ν​4ρU2L​[f′(∞)]2f′′(0)​.​
(80)
Our normalization has f′(∞)=1, so the displayed denominator is one. The factor four refers to both faces; for a plate wetted on only one face the drag is half this value.

Substitution of ei(kx−ωt) gives the dispersion relation ω(k)=Uk+k3​. The phase velocity is U+k2, whereas the group velocity is U+3k2. Thus nonzero-wavenumber crests move more slowly than their wave packet; the velocities coincide at zero wavenumber.
Fourier evolution gives ϕ(Vt,t)=∫A(k)eitΦ(k)dk, where Φ(k)=(V−U)k−k3. For V>U the two nondegenerate stationary points are k=±κ, κ=(V−U)/3​. At these points Φ(±κ)=±2κ3 and Φ′′(±κ)=∓6κ. Expanding the phase quadratically near each point and evaluating the oscillatory Gaussian integral gives the stationary phase method
ϕ(Vt,t)∼3κtπ​​[A(κ)ei(2κ3t−π/4)+A(−κ)e−i(2κ3t−π/4)].​
(81)
For a real initial field, A(−κ)=A(κ)​, so the two terms are conjugate. The approximation assumes a sufficiently smooth decaying amplitude; if a leading coefficient vanishes, the next stationary-phase terms determine that contribution.
For V<U, Φ′(k)=V−U−3k2<0 everywhere. There are no real stationary points, so no leading propagating packet reaches such a ray. For a Schwartz amplitude, repeated integration by parts with eitΦ=(itΦ′)−1∂k​eitΦ makes the contribution O(t−N) for every fixed N. With weaker data the decay rate depends on their regularity. This agrees with the minimum group velocity being U.

k2​=f+hf′f+h2(af′2f+21​f′′f2)+O(h3).

yn+1​=y+hf+21​h2f′f+h3(2a​f′2f+41​f′′f2)+O(h4).

R(z)=1−az1+(1−a)z+(1/2−a)z2​.​

If a=1/2, the quadratic numerator gives unbounded magnitude as z→−∞; when a=0 the denominator is constant and the same conclusion holds. Thus a=1/2 is necessary. At this value R(z)=(1+z/2)/(1−z/2), whose only pole is at positive z=2. Moreover
∣1−z/2∣2−∣1+z/2∣2=−2Rez≥0
